transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Start: 09:28 PDT
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood Product), Tom Herrera (CTO, Pinnacle), Nina Zhang (ML Eng), Aaron Blake (Platform), Priya Rao (Security)

Auto-generated summary: walk through parity map for three vendor stack, highlight gaps, propose bench and trial.

---
Topics: parity mapping, streaming, function calls, VPC, SOC2, perf tests, cost levers.

Action items (auto): see manual action items.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Lena from Redwood, with Raj and Maya. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Tom Herrera: Good, thanks. Running a bit behind on the morning stand but all good.
[00:13] Nina Zhang: Hey, hi, good to be here.
[00:15] Lena Park: Awesome. So goal today is a hands-on walkthrough for migrating from a mixed OpenAI/Anthropic/Together backend to Redwood API, parity mapping, and suggested steps for a trial. We'll try to cover streaming, function-calls, and private deployment questions.
[00:30] Raj Patel: I'll jump into a quick mapping table then demo the console and Optimize tips.
[00:37] Tom Herrera: Quick context — our prod now fans out to all three vendors depending on model. We have about 30 qps average, spikes ~120 qps, and typical sequences 120-800 tokens. We also do a lot of tool-calling via function-like contracts.
[00:49] Aaron Blake: We push through a gateway, and we operate inside GCP but need data residency for some PHI-adjacent workloads.
[00:57] Priya Rao: And security — we require SOC2, SSO/SAML, and KMS integration. On-prem or VPC would be preferred for certain datasets.
[01:05] Lena Park: Great context, thanks. Raj, can you show parity mapping?
[01:12] Raj Patel: Yep. So most of the OpenAI/Anthropic endpoints map directly to Redwood's generation and chat endpoints. A few gotchas: Together's streaming chunks are slightly different — timing and chunk boundaries — but Redwood supports both chunked streaming and token-level streaming. For function calls, Redwood's structured output support is compatible but you need to map the function schema; we'll show example code.
[01:35] Raj Patel: (screen share) Here's a snippet converting an OpenAI-style function call: change 'name' to the Redwood call target, ensure the schema is flattened in the payload. If you use Anthropic's Claude tool chain with 'tool' objects, map to Redwood's tool connectors — we provide a thin adapter.
[01:51] Nina Zhang: How about KV cache? We cache prefixes on the client side; we rely on model-side KV for long contexts. Does Redwood preserve KV state across calls or is it per-request?
[02:03] Raj Patel: Redwood has a KV cache layer in the runtime — it's controllable. You can pass a session id to reuse KV across requests, and we do prefix caching automatically if your pattern is repetitive. For private deployments we expose the same semantics; for hosted we have tenant separation.
[02:24] Tom Herrera: Latency is a big one. OpenAI's p95 for our short calls is around 120ms, Anthropic's a bit higher. How close can Redwood get in hosted mode versus Dedicated?
[02:34] Maya Chen: Short answer — hosted can get close in most cases but Dedicated gives you predictability. We tune kernels, batching, and sequence placement based on live profile. For Pinnacle's traffic shape — lots of 120-800 tokens — we'd recommend an initial Dedicated trial for benching to hit your p95 target consistently.
[02:53] Aaron Blake: Cost is a factor — if Dedicated has a large commit, we need to be confident about unit economics. What levers do we have?
[03:02] Raj Patel: Batching, automatic KV/prefix caching, and quantization profiles. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-route quantization that keeps quality within your eval thresholds but lowers token compute by 30-50% depending on model.
[03:19] [00:03:30] Speaker 1: (mumble) -- can you show a sample config of the rollout?
[03:24] Raj Patel: Sure. (screen) In the Console we show per-route model pinning, canary percentages, and an automatic fallback chain. So you can route 10% traffic to a cheaper quantized model and 90% to a higher quality variant. If latency spikes, fallback to another region or model variant.
[03:44] Priya Rao: For compliance, how are audit logs surfaced? We need immutable logs and KMS-wrapped keys.
[03:51] Lena Park: We emit audit logs to your cloud logging sink for Private, and for Dedicated we can stream audit logs to your project. Keys can be customer-managed via KMS/HSM integrations. SOC2 report will be in the pack we send.
[04:06] Priya Rao: Good. Also SSO and RBAC?
[04:09] Raj Patel: SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and granular RBAC in the console. We can demo that in a follow-up CSM session.
[04:20] Tom Herrera: About function calls— we have a complex orchestrator that calls tools and then reconciles outputs. Any differences in payload ordering or new error modes to watch for?
[04:31] Raj Patel: Redwood returns structured outputs in a JSON block similar to OpenAI function outputs. One difference: we may return 'partial' structured outputs during streaming; handle that by buffering until the 'done' sentinel. We've seen customers initially trip on that when they expect a single sync response.
[04:49] Nina Zhang: Does Redwood support hallucination controls or guard rails out of the box? We run classification post-processors now.
[04:55] Maya Chen: We have built-in tools for safety filters and you can plug in eval sets to Optimize so we can measure quality regressions for any model/quantization change. We also support reranking flows if you want deterministic first-pass then rerank.
[05:12] Aaron Blake: For our benchmark we need a deterministic test harness. Can Redwood run our synthetic load with the same traffic patterns?
[05:20] Raj Patel: Yes — we can spin up a dedicated bench with pinned models and replay your requests (with anonymized data). We'll coordinate an S3 drop of logs or you can stream them to our bench runner.
[05:33] [00:05:45] Speaker 2: (overlap) question about latency distribution across seq lengths?
[05:37] Raj Patel: We provided an example latency by length chart in the console; for long sequences you can expect higher variance but Dedicated reduces variance significantly. Our runtime picks kernels based on seq length distribution which helps tight p95.
[05:50] Tom Herrera: Is there an easy way to split routes between hosted and Dedicated? We might want to keep low-risk traffic on hosted and move PHI-adjacent to Dedicated.
[05:59] Raj Patel: Yes — routing policy supports per-route tiering. You can mark routes as "sensitive" and route to Dedicated or private deployment. Failover policies also let hosted take over if Dedicated is down, or vice versa, depending on your SLA preference.
[06:14] Nina Zhang: About streaming and webhooks: our existing implementation uses Together's server-sent events pattern. Will we need to rewrite stream handlers?
[06:23] Raj Patel: Small changes only. We support SSE and chunked HTTP, and the console will show example client adapters. We'll include a small shim in the runbook to translate Together SSE to Redwood stream frames.
[06:36] Lena Park: (quick note) We'll share a repo with config snippets for OpenAI->Redwood, Anthropic->Redwood, Together->Redwood mapping.
[06:43] Tom Herrera: Nice. On data residency: we need EU-only data for some customers. Do you have region pinning?
[06:50] Maya Chen: Yes. Hosted supports regional model routing; Dedicated can be deployed in EU-only regions, and Private gives you full control.
[06:58] Priya Rao: If we go Private, what are the minimum infra requirements? We may need an air-gapped option for certain customers.
[07:05] Raj Patel: For Private we support VPC and on-prem. Minimum is typically 4x A100-equivalent GPUs for initial deployment but it depends on model family and throughput. For air-gapped we have an on-prem installer; ops will share disk/network footprints.
[07:21] Aaron Blake: Okay that's helpful. For the bench, what model families do you recommend we test first? We currently use GPT-style 2.7–4-ish variants and a few Anthropic medium models.
[07:31] Raj Patel: Start with the closest open models we provide in our catalog — we can map to Redwood-verified performance profiles. For parity tests, pick the family that matches your current quality bar, then run quantization experiments via Optimize.
[07:46] [00:08:00] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) do you have examples of cost delta?
[07:50] Maya Chen: We have case studies in the deck showing 20-45% token compute reduction after applying caching and per-route quantization, with small quality impact controlled by eval thresholds.
[08:03] Tom Herrera: Let's talk timeline — we want to be ready for a pilot in 6–8 weeks ideally. Is that realistic?
[08:12] Lena Park: Yes — typical flow: 1) security review + SOC2 docs (1 week), 2) bench/proof-of-concept (2–3 weeks), 3) pilot with canary rollout (2–3 weeks). So 6–8 weeks is achievable if we start benching quickly.
[08:28] Priya Rao: We'll need the SOC2 and KMS integration details before infra review.
[08:33] Lena Park: Understood — we'll email those today.
[08:36] Nina Zhang: One more technical question — how does Redwood handle tokenization differences? We occasionally see token count diffs between vendors. If tokenization differs our cost math breaks.
[08:47] Raj Patel: We expose tokenization metrics and can run tokenization parity checks as part of the bench. Also, Optimize includes tokenization-aware cost estimates so you can see expected token deltas.
[08:58] Aaron Blake: For the bench, can you mimic our gateway and caching semantics? We have an edge cache that pads responses and we want to ensure interplay with Redwood caching doesn't double-cache.
[09:10] Raj Patel: We'll partner with your platform team (Aaron) to mirror gateway semantics. We usually run the bench in your network or in an isolated VPC to replicate behaviors.
[09:20] Tom Herrera: Sounds good. Any other blockers from Redwood side?
[09:23] Maya Chen: None immediate. We do need the traffic profile and any restricted dataset constraints for bench.
[09:30] [00:09:40] Speaker 3: (brief) question about training vs inference — not in scope today.
[09:34] Lena Park: Right — today is inference migration only.
[09:36] Raj Patel: Quick console tour — (screen) this is the dashboard, per-route token cost, per-token latency breakdown, and the Optimize suggestions panel. Here you can see suggested batch sizes and quantization profiles per route.
[09:53] Raj Patel: (narrating) If I click into a given route, you see model pins, rollout history, and test harness to replay sample prompts. You can attach eval sets and get regression alerts.
[10:06] Nina Zhang: The replay tool — will it accept our full payloads including tool calls?
[10:11] Raj Patel: Yes — you can upload sample requests; the runner will execute them against the pinned model and return logs identical to production responses.
[10:18] Tom Herrera: For billing and cost visibility, will we get per-route token attribution and customer-level breakdowns?
[10:25] Maya Chen: Yes — Console has token-level cost, per-route, and you can export CSVs to feed your internal chargeback. Dedicated has commit reconciliation reports.
[10:33] Aaron Blake: If we move forward with Dedicated trial, what's the minimum commitment?
[10:37] Lena Park: For trials we do a short-term reserved pool for benchmarks — not a full annual commit. We'll outline options in the quote.
[10:44] Priya Rao: Anything about data retention? We need to ensure logs are auto-purged for PHI flows.
[10:50] Raj Patel: Retention policies are configurable per-route and per-deployment. For Private you control retention entirely. For hosted we support retention settings and can purge or disable retention for sensitive routes.
[10:59] Tom Herrera: Great. Let's recap next steps and owners.
[11:03] Lena Park: Recap: we'll send SOC2 pack and KMS notes (Lena), Raj will post migration runbook and code snippets, Ops will provision trial Dedicated for bench, Pinnacle to send traffic profile. We'll schedule bench week of May 20.
[11:18] Nina Zhang: Sounds good. Anything else?
[11:20] Tom Herrera: No. Thanks, very helpful.
[11:22] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and calendar invites.
[11:26] (meeting ends)
